title: Blitzkrieg
subject: histoire
description: In **six weeks**, from **May 10** to **June 22, 1940**, the German army conquered France and the Benelux countries. This “lightning war” rewrote the art of war through sheer speed.

hero.hook: Six weeks to bring down what everyone thought was the best army in Europe.

blocks.text: From **May 10** to **June 22, 1940**, in just six weeks, the German army conquered France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg. Europe's leading military power collapsed in front of the whole world.
The **Blitzkrieg** (lightning war) was not simply a run of victories. It was a revolution: speed and the enemy's confusion mattered more than destroying his forces outright.

The word Blitzkrieg was never official inside the [[Wehrmacht]], the German armed forces from 1935 to 1945. The English-language press invented it. The Germans spoke of a war of movement. The principle behind it was the [[Schwerpunkt]]: throw everything at one narrow point to break the front.
The sirens on the Stukas, the dive bombers nicknamed “Jericho trumpets,” had no real military use. They were there only to terrify soldiers and civilians.

Where the French spread their tanks out to support the infantry, the Germans grouped them into independent armored divisions linked by radio. The Stukas worked as flying artillery. Meanwhile France still trusted the [[Maginot Line]], that chain of forts along the German border.

On the advice of General **Erich von Manstein**, Hitler adopted the [[Sichelschnitt]], the “sickle cut”: draw the Allies into Belgium while the bulk of the panzers, the German tanks, crossed the **Ardennes**, judged impassable. On **May 13**, General **Heinz Guderian** crossed the Meuse at **Sedan**. The road to the Channel was open.

Within a week the Allied armies were encircled, their backs to the sea. [[Operation Dynamo (Dunkirk)]] evacuated **338,000** French and British soldiers. Britain saved its army. France was left alone.

Stripped of its best divisions, France collapsed. Paris was declared an open city on **June 14**. Marshal **Philippe Pétain** asked for an armistice, signed on **June 22** at Compiègne, in the same railway car as in **1918**: Hitler was staging his revenge.
For the ceremony, Hitler had the railway car pulled out of the Compiègne museum and put back exactly where Germany had surrendered 22 years earlier.
On **June 18**, from London, **General de Gaulle** made his appeal on the BBC: France had lost a battle, not the war. The immediate effect was small. The foundations of Free France were laid.

1940 made Germany master of Europe. But the Blitzkrieg was a strategy built for a short war: limited fuel, fragile supply lines. In **1941**, facing the sheer size of the Soviet Union, it bogged down. The historian **Marc Bloch** would call the collapse a “Strange Defeat”: a French failure of thinking as much as of equipment.

events.title: Offensive in the West
events.detail: A simultaneous attack on the Benelux and a breakthrough in the Ardennes.

blocks.text: In six weeks the Blitzkrieg combined tanks, aircraft and radio to shatter a defensive doctrine. Speed and concentration of force beat the Maginot Line.
